<METHOD_NAME>Semantic Equivalence Masking via Constraint Satisfaction</METHOD_NAME>
<METHOD_DESCRIPTION>The problem is reframed from explicitly checking for a 3-clique ('any two materials chosen from the set correspond to a prohibited pair') to an equivalent constraint satisfaction property ('impossible to assign them to two vessels'). Surface pattern matchers will fixate on the 'two vessels' framing and attempt to deploy generic bipartite-checking or 2-SAT algorithms (like BFS for odd cycles), which struggle to efficiently enforce the exact subset size of 3 and the strict lexicographical minimization. Genuine reasoners will deduce that a 3-variable 2-coloring fails if and only if it is a 3-clique, and will confidently implement the correct, efficient triangle-enumerating algorithm.</METHOD_DESCRIPTION>
<METHOD_NOVEL>yes</METHOD_NOVEL>

<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Cargo Prohibition Protocol

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

A logistics firm operates a dual-vessel shipping route for hazardous materials. Certain pairs of these materials are highly reactive and are strictly prohibited from sharing a vessel.

The proposed loading schedule is structurally impossible to fulfill. You must produce a definitive proof of this impossibility to trigger an automatic schedule rejection.

To establish this proof, you are required to isolate a "deadlock" configuration of exactly three materials. A set of three materials constitutes a deadlock if it is impossible to assign them to the two vessels without violating the explicit prohibitions among them. Specifically, when considered in isolation, the subset of prohibitions strictly between these three materials must be sufficient to prevent any valid two-vessel assignment.

Because the automated auditing system requires deterministic reporting, it will not accept an arbitrary deadlock configuration. The system demands the canonical proof, meaning you must systematically ensure no earlier configuration could have been reported.

## Input
The first line provides two integers $n$ and $m$ ($3 \le n \le 2000$, $3 \le m \le \min(n(n-1)/2, 2 \cdot 10^5)$), indicating the number of hazardous materials and the number of prohibited pairs. The materials are identified by integers from $1$ to $n$.
Each of the following $m$ lines contains two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le n$, $u \ne v$) — a pair of materials that are prohibited from sharing a vessel. 
It is guaranteed that the input contains at least one deadlock configuration of three materials.

## Output
Output a single line containing three integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ ($a < b < c$), representing the identifiers of the materials in the deadlock configuration.
To satisfy the deterministic auditing system, if more than one such configuration exists, you must output the lexicographically earliest one among all valid configurations. This means you must minimize $a$; if there is a tie, minimize $b$; and if still tied, minimize $c$.

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
Changed the explicit requirement of "all pairs being prohibited" into the logically equivalent property of "unsatisfiable in a 2-vessel assignment". This forces the model to reason about what makes a 3-element subset not 2-colorable (which is exactly a 3-clique), rather than pattern-matching a direct description of a triangle.
</RATIONALE>
<PRESERVED_ANSWER>
A subset of exactly three vertices in a graph is not 2-colorable if and only if all three edges between them are present, so the set of valid configurations (and thus the lexicographically smallest one) is identical.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
<PRESERVED_CLASS>
The underlying task remains finding a 3-clique (triangle) in an undirected graph, keeping the complexity class unchanged.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
<RISK>
Models might misinterpret "impossible to assign them to the two vessels" as applying to the global graph rather than the isolated 3-element subset, though the text explicitly states "when considered in isolation, the subset of prohibitions strictly between these three materials must be sufficient".
</RISK>

<METHOD_NAME>Operational Chain of Implications</METHOD_NAME>
<METHOD_DESCRIPTION>Replaced the static definition of a mutually excluded triplet with an operational narrative of forced vessel assignments that loop back on themselves, disguising the structure of a 3-clique as a logical chain of deductions.</METHOD_DESCRIPTION>
<METHOD_NOVEL>yes</METHOD_NOVEL>

<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Cargo Prohibition Protocol

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

A logistics firm operates a dual-vessel shipping route for hazardous materials. Certain materials are highly reactive and are strictly prohibited from sharing a cargo hold.

The proposed loading schedule is structurally impossible to fulfill. You must produce a definitive proof of this impossibility to trigger an automatic schedule rejection.

To establish this proof, you are required to isolate a "deadlock" configuration. A deadlock is a specific group of exactly three distinct materials that creates an unresolvable placement chain. If you attempt to place the first material of the group in the port vessel, its documented reactivity with the second material of the group forces the second into the starboard vessel. If the second material has a documented reactivity with the third material of the group, the third is forced back into the port vessel. Finally, if the third material also has a documented reactivity with the first material, it cannot be placed in the port vessel either, proving no valid assignment to the two vessels can exist.

Because the automated auditing system requires deterministic reporting, it will not accept an arbitrary deadlock configuration. The system demands the canonical proof. When you identify a deadlock group of three materials, you must sort their identifiers in ascending order to form a sequence. Among all possible deadlock groups in the manifest, you must report the one whose sorted sequence is lexicographically earliest.

## Input
The first line provides two integers $n$ and $m$. The integer $n$ represents the number of hazardous materials; the manifest protocol requires at least three materials, while the physical capacity of the loading dock limits this to two thousand. The integer $m$ represents the number of documented reactive pairs; the safety database requires at least three logged interactions, up to a strict storage limit of two hundred thousand records (or the maximum possible number of unique pairs for the given materials, whichever is smaller). The materials are identified by integers from $1$ to $n$.
Each of the following $m$ lines contains two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le n$, $u \ne v$) — indicating that material $u$ and material $v$ are reactive and cannot share a vessel. 
It is guaranteed that the input contains at least one deadlock configuration of three materials.

## Output
Output a single line containing three integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ ($a < b < c$), representing the identifiers of the materials in the canonical deadlock configuration.

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
The direct description of a set of three mutually prohibited materials was replaced with an operational narrative detailing how assigning them to two vessels creates a logical contradiction. This forces the model to deduce that the described chain of forced assignments corresponds to a 3-clique (triangle) in the graph of prohibitions, rather than relying on explicit keywords.
</RATIONALE>
<PRESERVED_ANSWER>
The condition for a deadlock remains exactly three materials where all three pairs are reactive, and the output is still the lexicographically earliest sorted triplet of such materials, ensuring identical results.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
<PRESERVED_CLASS>
The core task is unchanged—finding the lexicographically smallest triangle in an undirected graph—so the time complexity and algorithm remain identical.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
<RISK>
none
</RISK>

expert_critique:
<CRITIQUE>
The gate rejection is correct: your draft subtly changed/dropped parts of the formal contract even though the story is good.

1. **Bounds need to be stated in the exact formal form from the seed.**  
   Your input section uses prose (“at least three… limits this to two thousand”) instead of the seed’s precise inequality block. Even if logically equivalent to a human, this often fails strict contract checks.  
   Also, you added explicit per-endpoint constraints `1 ≤ u, v ≤ n` and `u ≠ v`, which are **not present** in the seed text. Adding constraints can change the legal input space.

2. **Tie-break rule is not explicit in seed form.**  
   You say “lexicographically earliest” after sorting, but the seed requires the exact deterministic tie-break wording:  
   - smallest `a`; ties by smallest `b`; then smallest `c`.  
   Some validators treat plain “lexicographically earliest” as insufficiently explicit.

3. **Output condition is under-specified in the Output section.**  
   Seed output requires not only `a < b < c`, but also explicitly that all three conflict pairs exist (`a-b`, `a-c`, `b-c`).  
   Your output section omits this explicit condition and relies on narrative inference (“deadlock configuration”). This weakens exactness.

4. **Risk of ambiguity from narrative mechanics.**  
   The long “port/starboard forcing chain” explanation is readable, but it can be interpreted as directional/logical process rather than the simple undirected triangle condition. For contract fidelity, the formal graph condition should be stated directly in one crisp sentence in Input/Output spec.
</CRITIQUE>

<PROPOSALS>
- Replace the first Input line prose with a formal bounds line matching seed structure exactly, e.g., explicitly present `3 ≤ n ≤ 2000` and `3 ≤ m ≤ min(n·(n−1)/2, 2·10^5)` in one place.
- Remove added constraints not in seed (`u ≠ v`, and even explicit `1 ≤ u,v ≤ n` if you keep strict fidelity), or move them to non-binding explanatory text that does not alter the contract.
- In Output, explicitly require: “print `a b c` with `a < b < c` **such that** pairs `a-b`, `a-c`, and `b-c` are conflicts.”
- Add the tie-break in seed’s explicit hierarchy form: “Among all valid triples, output the lexicographically smallest one (smallest `a`; if tied, smallest `b`; if tied, smallest `c`).”
- Keep the cargo narrative, but separate “story” from a strict formal block so validators can unambiguously detect unchanged I/O rules.
- Ensure the guarantee sentence mirrors seed precisely: “It is guaranteed that at least one such triple exists.”
</PROPOSALS>

<KEEP>
- The re-themed narrative is coherent and engaging.
- You correctly preserve the core task as finding a 3-item conflict clique (triangle), not constructing a full 2-way assignment.
- Examples are preserved and consistent with expected outputs.
- Deterministic-output intent (“canonical proof”) is good; just tighten the formal tie-break wording.
</KEEP>

<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Cargo Prohibition Protocol

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

A logistics firm operates a dual-vessel shipping route for hazardous materials. Certain pairs of these materials are highly reactive when stored in the same vessel and are strictly prohibited from sharing a cargo hold.

For any material $x$, let $P(x)$ denote the set of materials that are explicitly prohibited from sharing a vessel with $x$ as given in the input. Note that this prohibition is symmetric; if $u$ and $v$ are a prohibited pair, then $u \in P(v)$ and $v \in P(u)$.

The proposed loading schedule is structurally impossible to fulfill. You must produce a definitive proof of this impossibility to trigger an automatic schedule rejection.

To establish this proof, you are required to isolate a "deadlock" configuration. A deadlock consists of exactly three distinct materials, denoted as $a, b,$ and $c$ (ordered such that $a < b < c$), which satisfy the following mutual inclusion conditions:
- $b$ is an element of $P(a)$
- $c$ is an element of $P(a)$
- $c$ is an element of $P(b)$

The presence of such a configuration demonstrates that no valid assignment to the two vessels can exist.

Because the automated auditing system requires deterministic reporting, it will not accept an arbitrary deadlock configuration. The system demands the canonical proof, meaning you must systematically ensure no earlier configuration could have been reported.

## Input
The first line provides two integers $n$ and $m$ ($3 \le n \le 2000$, $3 \le m \le \min(n(n-1)/2, 2 \cdot 10^5)$), indicating the number of hazardous materials and the number of prohibited pairs. The materials are identified by integers from $1$ to $n$.
Each of the following $m$ lines contains two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le n$, $u \ne v$) — a pair of materials that are prohibited from sharing a vessel. 
It is guaranteed that the input contains at least one deadlock configuration of three materials.

## Output
Output a single line containing three integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ ($a < b < c$), representing the identifiers of the materials in the deadlock configuration.
To satisfy the deterministic auditing system, if more than one such configuration exists, you must output the one that minimizes the first identifier $a$. If there are multiple valid configurations tied for the smallest $a$, break the tie by minimizing the second identifier $b$. If there is still a tie, minimize the third identifier $c$.

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
The description of the triangle (3-clique) was rewritten from a pairwise graph property ("any two materials chosen from the set") into a set-theoretic mutual inclusion property ($b \in P(a)$, $c \in P(a)$, $c \in P(b)$). This removes the linguistic triggers for standard graph algorithms while explicitly guiding reasoning models toward the intended set-intersection (bitset) solution. All numeric bounds and tie-breaking rules were restored precisely to their original formal structures to ensure strict contract fidelity.
</RATIONALE>
<PRESERVED_ANSWER>
The set inclusion conditions $b \in P(a)$, $c \in P(a)$, and $c \in P(b)$ for $a < b < c$ are mathematically identical to requiring all three edges of a triangle to exist, meaning the exact same subsets of materials are identified as deadlocks.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
<PRESERVED_CLASS>
The problem still requires finding a 3-clique (triangle) in an undirected graph, which serves as a certificate of non-bipartiteness, keeping it in the same complexity class.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
<RISK>
none
</RISK>
